The laundromat on Delancey Street was the only place open between the 24-hour bodega on the corner and the parking garage four blocks south. Mara found it the way you find a tooth when it's the only one left. Necessity. The kind that doesn't argue with you.

She'd been walking for three hours. Not running, not really. Just walking with the particular purposelessness of someone who needed her legs to do something while her mind was doing something else. Her hands were in her coat pockets, and inside the pockets, her fingers kept finding the ring. Not the engagement ring. She'd sold that one in November, back when David still set two mugs on the counter even though he'd only drink one. The ring she kept in her pocket now was small, silver, dented. Her mother's. The one from the box in the kitchen drawer that had no note, no card, no explanation. Just a ring and a drawer that was lighter than it had been.

The laundromat smelled like warm wool and lemon industrial cleaner. There were six machines in a row, and only one was running. The light from it pulsed blue-white, and the sound was that low mechanical hum that somehow felt like breathing. A machine breathing. She pulled a chair from near the register, the plastic kind that wobbles on three legs and rests the fourth in perpetual midair, and she sat.

Nobody else was here. Not that it was unusual. Two in the morning was laundromat's small hours. The owner, if there was one, had a cot behind the glass partition. The glass was fogged with steam from somewhere inside, and a single fluorescent tube buzzed above it, flickering in that almost-rhythmic way that made your eyes want to look away.

Mara pulled her coat off and draped it over the chair back. Underneath, she wore a grey sweater that was two sizes too big. She hadn't ironed it. She hadn't done much of anything in four days. The apartment was... not empty. Empty implied a choice. What it was, was full of the specific negative space where a person had been. The dent in the couch cushion. The coffee ring on the end table, wiped and re-applied, a little ritual of faith. The two mugs. One of them was chipped. She kept the chipped one. She didn't know why. Probably because the whole one felt too complete, too finished. The chipped one had a story. A small accident in a small life.

She loaded the machine. Socks, towels, a bedsheet that was too big for the drum and crumpled in on itself like a letter that had been folded and refolded and folded again until the words were illegible. She set the dial to warm. She pressed the button. The machine shuddered, caught, and began its slow rotation. The clothes tumbled in a way that was almost like a small, contained storm.

She sat back down. She put her feet up on the empty plastic chair in front of her. She looked at the other machines and thought about how they were all identical and how that was a kind of loneliness. Same shape, same function, same hum. But each one held a different someone's dirty things. Someone's t-shirt with the small stain on the collar. Someone's child's dress with the missing button. Someone's good shirt, the one you only wore for the occasions you'd decided not to have any more of.

The ring in her pocket caught her attention. She pulled it out. Held it up to the blue light. The dent in it was a small valley, and in the valley, the metal was a slightly different color. Tarnished. Worn. Her mother had worn it for forty years. Forty years of a small metal circle going around a small bone. The ring didn't know she was dead. The ring just kept being a ring. It didn't need to know. It just kept its shape, and its shape was the only prayer it had.

Mara put it back in her pocket. She watched the machines turn. The blue light pulsed. The fluorescent tube buzzed and flickered. Somewhere, a pipe knocked twice, like a small knuckle on a door.

She thought: *I will wash the sheets. I will dry the towels. I will carry everything home in the plastic bags that smell like the dryer sheets, the ones that say Lavender Fields but smell like nothing quite like a field. I will hang the sheets up. I will make the bed. I will sleep in the chipped-mug apartment. And in the morning, I will make coffee. One cup. And I will drink it standing at the counter, and I will look out the window at the fire escape, and the morning will be just a morning, and I will be just a woman in a grey sweater who needed to wash a bedsheet.*

And that would be enough. That would be the whole of it. Not the story. Not the arc. Not the lesson. Just the next small thing. The next machine, filling up and emptying out. The next small thing, filling up and emptying out. The next small thing.

The machine buzzed. Done.

Mara stood up. Her knees cracked. She pulled the clothes out, still warm, still turning, and they smelled like clean cotton and the particular warm smell of things that have been tumbling in hot water and air. She folded the bedsheet on top of the towels. She tied the knots in the plastic bag. She walked to the register, put down the coins, and stepped outside into the cold.

The street was empty. The bodega was still open, its windows glowing yellow and a little too bright. The parking garage was a rectangle of concrete and shadow. The sky above was the flat, undetailed grey of a city at two in the morning, where the stars have given up and the moon is just another small hum in the dark.

She walked home. She walked the way she'd walked to get here. Slow. Purposeless. Her hands in her pockets. Her fingers finding the ring.

The ring kept its shape.

The morning was still hours away.

She'd been walking for three hours. Not running, not really. Just walking with the particular purposelessness of someone who needed her legs to do something while her mind was doing something else. Her hands were in her coat pockets, and inside the pockets, her fingers kept finding the ring. Not the engagement ring. She'd sold that one in November, back when the apartment was still warm and the radiator clanked its evening complaint and David still set two mugs on the counter even though he'd only drink one. The ring she kept in her pocket now was small, silver, dented. Her mother's. The one from the box in the kitchen drawer that had no note, no card, no explanation. Just a ring and a drawer that was lighter than it had been.

The laundromat smelled like warm wool and lemon industrial cleaner. There were six machines in a row, and only one was running. The light from it pulsed blue-white, and the sound was that low mechanical hum that somehow felt like breathing. A machine breathing. She pulled a chair from near the register, the plastic kind that wobbles on three legs and rests the fourth in perpetual midair, and she sat.

Nobody else was here. Not that it was unusual. Two in the morning was laundromat's small hours. The owner, if there was one, had a cot behind the glass partition. The glass was fogged with steam from somewhere inside, and a single fluorescent tube buzzed above it, flickering in that almost-rhythmic way that made your eyes want to look away.

Mara pulled her coat off and draped it over the chair back. Underneath, she wore a grey sweater that was two sizes too big. She hadn't ironed it. She hadn't done much of anything in four days. The apartment was... not empty. Empty implied a choice. What it was, was full of the specific negative space where a person had been. The dent in the couch cushion. The coffee ring on the end table that she kept wiping and re-applying to, a little ritual of faith. The two mugs. One of them was chipped. She kept the chipped one. She didn't know why. Probably because the whole one felt too complete, too finished. The chipped one had a story. A small accident in a small life.

She loaded the machine. Socks, towels, a bedsheet that was too big for the drum and crumpled in on itself like a letter that had been folded and refolded and folded again until the words were illegible. She set the dial to warm. She pressed the button. The machine shuddered, caught, and began its slow rotation. The clothes tumbled in a way that was almost like a small, contained storm.

She sat back down. She put her feet up on the empty plastic chair in front of her. She looked at the other machines and thought about how they were all identical and how that was a kind of loneliness. Same shape, same function, same hum. But each one held a different someone's dirty things. Someone's t-shirt with the small stain on the collar. Someone's child's dress with the missing button. Someone's good shirt, the one you only wore for the occasions you'd decided not to have any more of.

The ring in her pocket caught her attention. She pulled it out. Held it up to the blue light. The dent in it was a small valley, and in the valley, the metal was a slightly different color. It didn't need to know. It just kept its shape, and its shape was the only prayer it had.

Mara put it back in her pocket. She watched the machines turn. The blue light pulsed. The fluorescent tube buzzed and flickered. Somewhere, a pipe knocked twice, like a small knuckle on a door.

She thought: I will wash the sheets. I will dry the towels. I will carry everything home in the plastic bags that smell like the dryer sheets, the ones that say Lavender Fields but smell like nothing quite like a field. I will hang the sheets up. I will make the bed. I will sleep in the chipped-mug apartment. And in the morning, I will make coffee. One cup. And I will drink it standing at the counter, and I will look out the window at the fire escape, and the fire escape will be just a fire escape, and the morning will be just a morning, and I will be just a woman in a grey sweater who needed to wash a bedsheet.

And that would be enough. That would be the whole of it. Not the story. Not the arc. Not the lesson. Just the next small thing. The next machine, filling up and emptying out. The next small thing, filling up and emptying out. The next small thing.

The machine buzzed. Done.

She pulled the clothes out, still warm, still turning, and they smelled like clean cotton and the particular warm smell of things that have been tumbling in hot water and air. She folded the bedsheet on top of the towels. She tied the knots in the plastic bag. She walked to the register, put down the coins, and stepped outside into the cold.

The street was empty. The bodega was still open, its windows glowing yellow and a little too bright. The parking garage was a rectangle of concrete and shadow. The sky above was the flat, undetailed grey of a city at two in the morning, where the stars have given up and the moon is just another light, another source, another small hum in the dark.

She walked home. She walked the way she'd walked to get here. Slow. Purposeless. Her hands in her pockets. Her fingers finding the ring.

The ring kept its shape.

The morning was still hours away."
